title: How TLS 1.3 sets up HTTPS in one round trip
purpose: See which messages a TLS 1.3 handshake sends, in what order, and why the browser can send its first request after one round trip.
sequence_reason: The handshake is an ordered chain of messages where each step depends on the one before (keys, then encryption, then proof), so motion shows the order and the round trips better than one static diagram.
summary: The browser sends ClientHello with a key share, the server name (SNI) and its application protocols (ALPN). The server replies with ServerHello and its key share, so both sides derive the same handshake keys. Everything after that is encrypted: EncryptedExtensions, Certificate, CertificateVerify and Finished. The browser checks the signature and the MAC, sends its own Finished, and sends its first HTTP request. That is one round trip. A returning browser with a pre-shared key can send early data in the first flight, but that data has no forward secrecy guarantee and can be replayed between connections.
explanation: Certificate says who the server claims to be, CertificateVerify proves that the server holds the private key, and Finished proves that nobody changed the handshake. Early data (0-RTT) saves one round trip but can be replayed, so send only requests that are safe to repeat.

learning_check.question: Which handshake message proves that the server holds the private key for its certificate, and why is the Certificate message alone not enough?
learning_check.answer: CertificateVerify. It is a signature over the handshake transcript made with the private key. Anyone can copy a certificate, but only the key holder can make that signature.

scenes.heading: One round trip to a secure channel
scenes.narration: Before the first HTTPS request, the browser and the server must agree on secret keys. TLS 1.3 does this in one round trip.

scenes.heading: ClientHello: key share, SNI, ALPN
scenes.narration: The browser sends ClientHello. It carries a key share, the server name, called SNI, and the protocols it speaks, called ALPN.

path.label: key_share + server_name (SNI) + ALPN: h2, http/1.1. Not encrypted.

scenes.heading: ServerHello: both sides now share keys
scenes.narration: The server answers with ServerHello and its own key share. Now both sides compute the same handshake keys. Neither side sends the keys.

path.label: Its key_share uses the same group as one client share.

scenes.heading: The encrypted server flight
scenes.narration: Everything after ServerHello is encrypted. The server sends EncryptedExtensions, which carries the chosen ALPN protocol, then Certificate, CertificateVerify and Finished.

path.label: First encrypted message: chosen ALPN protocol.

scenes.heading: What each message proves
scenes.narration: Certificate names the server. Anyone can copy a certificate, so CertificateVerify signs the transcript with the private key. Finished proves that nobody changed the handshake.

items: Certificate: who the server says it is
CertificateVerify: the server holds the private key
Any check fails: the browser aborts

scenes.heading: Client Finished, then the request
scenes.narration: The browser checks the signature and the MAC, then sends its own Finished. Its first HTTP request follows at once as encrypted application data.

path.label: The client confirms the same transcript.
Application data under new traffic keys.

scenes.heading: Count the trips: 1-RTT
scenes.narration: Count the trips. One flight goes out, one flight comes back, then the request leaves. That is one round trip. A key share mismatch adds a second trip.

scenes.heading: 0-RTT early data and replay
scenes.narration: A returning browser can skip the wait. With a pre-shared key from an earlier visit, it sends early data in the first flight. An attacker can replay that data, so send only safe requests.

right.label: 0-RTT early data
items: Sent in the first flight with a PSK

visual.verdict: Send early data only when a replay does no harm.
